power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We expected a large effect size for the correlational hypotheses (r = .50), a medium effect size for the regression hypotheses (R² = .12), and d = 0.60 (based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022) for the difference hypotheses. Based on these a priori power considerations, the target sample size was N = 100 in order to achieve at least .90 power. Initially, 77 first-year students participated in the experiment. We excluded eight participants due to technical issues or problems with the think-aloud procedure or preregistered criteria, namely, a reported lack of commitment, resulting in 69 valid cases (83% female; 16% male, 1% nonbinary; age: M = 20.2, SD = 2.4). With N = 69, we could still achieve an acceptable power of ≥ .80 for all analyses.
For the difference hypotheses, we could achieve only .58 power, but based on the results from Study 1, we could expect larger effect sizes (d = .90), resulting in acceptable power (.86).

As in Study 1, the study followed a one-factorial design with preparation activity as the between-subjects factor. Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions and either invented a solution (high-generative, n = 19) or self-explained a worked-out solution (low-generative, n = 20). As in Study 1, all participants were psychology students at a German university in the first semester of a Bachelor's degree program and received course credit for their participation. All participants gave informed consent before taking part. The experiment was approved by the university's ethics board and preregistered at OSF (https://osf.io/wajne/overview?view_only=9f4ae2374f204f69bb861d041db8a398). We expected large effects for the correlational hypotheses (r = .50), R² = .09 (based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2015) and the regression hypotheses and d = 0.60 (based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022) for the difference hypotheses. On the basis of these a priori power considerations, the targeted sample size was N = 90 in order to achieve at least .83 power in all analyses. Initially, 44 first-year students participated in the experiment, but we had to exclude 5 participants due to technical issues, problems with the think-aloud procedure, or preregistered criteria, namely, a reported lack of commitment, resulting in only 39 valid cases (82% female; 10% male, 8% nonbinary; age: M = 20.9, SD = 3.2). Therefore, our sample size was much smaller than planned, but it did not affect the correlational hypotheses with .97 power with the sample size of N = 39.

table.title: Measuring intermediate deep feature knowledge in preparation for learning
table.research_questions:
1) Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity: 
1a) We expect a high positive correlation between our recognition test and the deep features measured with think-aloud.
1b) We expect a high positive correlation between self-reported deep feature recognition and the deep features measured with think-aloud.


2) Difference Hypotheses: Generally, we expect learners’ recognition of deep features to be higher in the worked example condition compared to learners in the inventing condition. More specifically:
2a) We expect that learners in the worked example condition elaborate more deep features (measured with think-aloud) compared to learners in the inventing condition. 
2b) We expect that learners in the worked example condition reach a higher score in the developed recognition test compared to learners in the inventing condition.
2c) We expect that learners in the worked example condition self-report a higher recognition of deep features compared to learners in the inventing condition.

3) Regression Hypotheses: We expect that learners’ deep feature recognition (measured with think-aloud) predicts learning outcome (near transfer, H3a and far transfer, H3b).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: Between subjects design with 1 factor (preparation activity) and 2 levels (inventing task vs. self-explanation of worked example)
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through advertisements in a first semester psychology lecture. Participants will receive a certificate of participation. Participants must be at least 18 years old and first year undergraduate students.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 100 participants.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size ist based on power considerations as well as time and personnel factors: We expect to be able to assess approximately 100 participants within our time and personnel ressources. With this sample size we could achieve .97 power for the regression hypotheses (expecting a medium effect R^2 = .13, α = .05) and .99 power for the correlation hypotheses as well as .90 power for the difference hypotheses (α = .05, expected d = .60 based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022), which is acceptable to us.
table.stopping_rule: As we can only assess students at the beginning of their studies, the maximum possible sample size is determined by the number of first year psychology students willing to participate.
table.manipulated_variables: We vary the preparation task that participants do before watching an instructional video. Participants either work through a solved problem (worked example) or try to find a solution on their own (inventing).
table.measured_variables:
We measure the following variables: 

learning outcome: We will measure the learning outcome after the instructional video with a post-test consisting of tasks on near transfer and far transfer of conceptual knowledge. 

Deep features: We will measure the processing of deep features with three measurements (think-aloud, recognition test and self-report). 
• Think-aloud: We will ask participants to speak-out their thoughts while working on the preparation task following the think-aloud procedure described by Ericsson & Simon, 1980. We will code the think-aloud protocols regarding the number of processed deep features as well as the level of processing of deep features. 
• Recognition test: We will measure the recognition of deep features with a recognition test after the preparation activity. The test consists of three items, each of which consists of three sets of images of diagrams. The sets are alienated variants of the original diagrams from the preparation activity. Each item contained only one set of diagrams that correctly represents a deep feature of the learning content (e.g., different number of data points). Participants are asked to decide which drawing most closely resembles the diagrams that were presented in the preparation phase. They are also asked to write a short explanation for their decision and to rate their certainty (on the scale very uncertain – uncertain – certain – very certain and the option “I guessed”).
• Self-report: We will measure the self-reported processing of deep features with a questionnaire at the end of the learning sequence. In this questionnaire, each deep feature is described, and participants are asked, if and when they first thought about that aspect. Therefore, they can choose one of the following options: “while working on the preparation task”, “during the questionnaire after the preparation activity”, “while working on the recognition task”, “while watching the instructional video”, “while working on the post-test”, “I never thought about this aspect”. 

We will also assess knowledge gap awareness, self-efficacy and epistemic curiosity using the questionnaires used in Glogger-Frey et al., 2015.
table.indices:
Learning outcome: We will sum up the achieved points in the post-test separately for near and for far transfer as measures for learning outcome. 

Deep Features – think-aloud: We will sum up the number of deep features that were elaborated. In addition, we will calculate the average level of processing for each participant. 

Deep Features – recognition test: We will count the number of correct recognitions. We will also count the number of correct reasoning of decisions. 

Deep Features – self-report: We will count the number of deep features that are self-reported as elaborated during the preparation activity.
table.statistical_tests:
Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity: 
We will calculate pearson correlation coefficients to analyse the convergent validity. We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of correctly recognized data sets in the recognition test and the number of correct reasoning in the recognition test (H1a). We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of self-reported elaborated deep features (H1b). 
In addition, we will check for differences of the correlation pattern between the inventing and the worked example subgroup and correct for them if necessary.

Difference Hypotheses 
We will use t-tests for two independent groups (Inventing vs. Worked Example) to analyse the differences in the number of elaborated deep features (H2a), recognition test score (H2b) and self-reported recognition of deep features (H2c)

Regression Hypotheses
We will run linear regression analyses with learning outcome (near transfer, far transfer) as dependent variables and deep features as independent variable. We will run separate regression analyses for each deep feature measurement (think-aloud, recognition test, self-report) as we expect a high correlation between them (multicollinearity). We expect similar result patterns for each deep feature measurement and will interpret this as an indicator of convergent validity.  
In addition, we will check for differences in the pattern of results between the inventing and worked example subgroups and correct for them if necessary.
table.transformations: We will code the think-aloud protocols as follows: In a first step, we will assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements. In a second step, we will determine the number of deep feature elements that were processed at a level of elaboration or higher.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p <.05 criteria for determining if the results significantly differ from those expected in the null hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants who report a lack of commitment will be excluded. Therefore, we have two control questions (one after the preparation activity and one after the post-test) in which participants are asked to rate their commitment. Participants who report less than 25% in one (or both) control questions will be excluded. 
We will also exclude participants who have problems with the think-aloud procedure (e.g. they seem very irritated/nervous about the procedure)
table.missing_data_handling: Only data from participants who completed the entire learning sequence will be included in the analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses: We plan to check for differences between the preparation activities regarding self-efficacy, epistemic curiosity and knowledge gap awareness for exploratory reasons.
table.additional_comments: We aim to use the data of this experiment to extend the sample size of another study where we could not reach the target sample size (see preregistration: https://osf.io/4tshq/?view_only=dfbdad9d7dca4e53940877d3daf9af21). Before merging the data, we will test whether the two subsamples differ systematically regarding age, gender and prior knowledge. We will only merge the data if there are no systematic differences between the subsamples.

table.title: Measuring intermediate deep feature knowledge in preparation for learning - Study 2
table.research_questions:
1. Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity: We expect a high positive correlation between our instruments for measuring intermediate deep feature knowledge and the think-aloud measurement: 
1a) high positive correlation between recognition test and think-aloud.
1b) high positive correlation between stimulated self-report and think-aloud.

2. Difference Hypotheses: Generally, we expect learners’ intermediate deep feature knowledge to be higher in the worked example condition compared to learners in the inventing condition. More specifically:
2a) Learners in the worked example condition show more elaborated deep features (measured via think-aloud) compared to learners in the inventing condition
2b) Learners in the worked example condition perform better in the recognition test compared to learners in the inventing condition
2c) Learners in the worked example condition self-report a higher elaboration of deep features during preparation compared to learners in the inventing condition.

3. Regression Hypotheses: We expect that learner's intermediate deep feature knowledge predicts learning outcomes. 
3a) Learners’ intermediate deep feature knowledge (measured via think-aloud) predicts learning outcomes.
3b) Learners’ score in the recognition test predicts learning outcomes.
3c) Learners’ self-reported deep feature elaboration predicts learning outcomes.

table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through advertisements in a first semester psychology lecture. Participants will receive a certificate of participation. Participants must be at least 18 years old and first year undergraduate students.
table.sample_size_rationale:
The target sample size is based on power considerations as well as time and personnel factors: We expect to be able to assess approximately 90 participants within our time and personnel resources. 
With N = 90 we could achieve .99 power for the correlation hypotheses (expecting a large effect size r = .5, α = .05) as well as .88 power for the difference hypotheses (α = .05, expected d = .60 based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022) and .83 power for the regression hypotheses (α = .05, expected R^2 = .09 based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2015) which is acceptable to us.
table.stopping_rule: As we can only assess students at the beginning of their studies, the maximum possible sample size is determined by the number of first year psychology students willing to participate.
table.manipulated_variables: We vary the preparation task that participants do before watching an instructional video. Participants either work through a solved problem (worked example) or try to find a solution on their own (inventing).
table.measured_variables:
We measure the following variables: 
learning outcome: We will measure the learning outcome after the instructional video with a post-test consisting of tasks on near transfer and far transfer of conceptual knowledge. 

Deep features: We will measure intermediate deep feature knowledge with three measurements (think-aloud, recognition test and stimulated self-report): 
•	Think-aloud: We will ask participants to speak-out their thoughts while working on the preparation task following the think-aloud procedure described by Ericsson & Simon, 1980. We will code the think-aloud protocols to assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements
•	Recognition test: We will measure the recognition of deep features with a recognition test after the preparation activity as a proxy of intermediate deep feature knowledge. The test consists of three items, each of which consists of three sets of images of diagrams. The sets are alienated variants of the original diagrams from the preparation activity. Each item contains only one set of diagrams that correctly represents a deep feature of the learning content (e.g., different number of data points). Participants are asked to decide which drawing most closely resembles the diagrams that were presented in the preparation phase. 
•	self-report: We will measure the self-reported processing of deep features as a proxy of intermediate deep feature knowledge with a questionnaire at the end of the learning sequence. The self-report is stimulated by a timeline showing the study phases graphically plus a miniature picture of the material to help learners to remember when and if they first elaborated on each deep feature. In this questionnaire, each deep feature is described, and participants are asked to choose one of the following options: “while working on the preparation task”, “during the questionnaire after the preparation activity”, “while working on the recognition task”, “while watching the instructional video”, “while working on the exercise tasks”, “I never thought about this aspect”. 

For exploratory reasons, we will also assess cognitive load (using the scales from Krieglstein et al., 2023), as well as self-efficacy and epistemic curiosity (using the questionaires from Glogger-Frey et al., 2015).
table.indices:
Learning outcome: We will sum up the achieved points in the post-test. 

Deep Features – think-aloud: We will assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements by adding up the number of deep features that were elaborated. 

Deep Features – recognition test: We will count the number of correct recognitions. 

Deep Features – self-report: We will count the number of deep features that are self-reported as elaborated during the preparation activity.
table.statistical_tests:
1. Correlation Hypotheses - convergent validity: 
We will calculate pearson correlation coefficients to analyse the convergent validity. We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of correctly recognised data sets in the recognition test (H1a) and with the number of self-reported elaborated deep features (H1b). 
In addition, we will check for differences in the correlation patterns between the inventing and the worked example subgroups and correct for them if necessary. 

2. Difference Hypotheses: 
We will use t-tests for two independent groups (Inventing vs. Worked Example) to analyse the differences in the number of elaborated deep features (H2a), recognition test score (H2b) and stimulated self-report score (H2c)

3.Regression Hypotheses: 
We will run linear regression analyses with learning outcomes as the dependent variable and deep features as the independent variable. As we expect high correlations between them (multicollinearity), we will run separate analyses for each deep feature measurement (H3a: think-aloud; H3b: recognition test; H3c: self-report). Similar result patterns for each measurement will be interpreted as an indicator of convergent validity. 
In addition, we will check for differences in the result patterns between the inventing and the worked example subgroups and correct for them if necessary.
table.transformations: We will code the think-aloud protocolls as follows: In a first step, we will assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements. The four levels of processing are: (1) naming - (2) naming+calculation - (3) elaboration - (4) elaboration + correct solution.  In a second step, we will determine the number of deep features that were processed at a level of elaboration or higher.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p = .05 criteria for determining if the results significantly differ from those expected in the null hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants who report a lack of commitment will be excluded. Therefore, we have two control questions (one after the preparation activity and one after the post-test) in which participants are asked to rate their commitment. Participants who report less than 25% in one (or both) control questions will be excluded. 
We will also exclude participants who have problems with the think-aloud procedure (e.g. they seem very irritated/nervous about the procedure).
table.missing_data_handling: Only data from participants who completed the entire learning sequence will be included in the analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses: We plan to assess cognitive load, mental effort, self-efficacy and epistemic curiosity for exploratory reasons.

table.title: Measuring intermediate deep feature knowledge in preparation for learning
table.research_questions:
1) Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity: 
1a) We expect a high positive correlation between our recognition test and the deep features measured with think-aloud.
1b) We expect a high positive correlation between self-reported deep feature recognition and the deep features measured with think-aloud.


2) Difference Hypotheses: Generally, we expect learners’ recognition of deep features to be higher in the worked example condition compared to learners in the inventing condition. More specifically:
2a) We expect that learners in the worked example condition elaborate more deep features (measured with think-aloud) compared to learners in the inventing condition. 
2b) We expect that learners in the worked example condition reach a higher score in the developed recognition test compared to learners in the inventing condition.
2c) We expect that learners in the worked example condition self-report a higher recognition of deep features compared to learners in the inventing condition.

3) Regression Hypotheses: We expect that learners’ deep feature recognition (measured with think-aloud) predicts learning outcome (near transfer, H3a and far transfer, H3b).

table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: Between subjects design with 1 factor (preparation activity) and 2 levels (inventing task vs. self-explanation of worked example)
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through advertisements in a first semester psychology lecture. Participants will receive a certificate of participation. Participants must be at least 18 years old and first year undergraduate students.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 100 participants.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size ist based on power considerations as well as time and personnel factors: We expect to be able to assess approximately 100 participants within our time and personnel ressources. With this sample size we could achieve .97 power for the regression hypotheses (expecting a medium effect R^2 = .13, α = .05) and .99 power for the correlation hypotheses as well as .90 power for the difference hypotheses (α = .05, expected d = .60 based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022), which is acceptable to us.
table.stopping_rule: As we can only assess students at the beginning of their studies, the maximum possible sample size is determined by the number of first year psychology students willing to participate.
table.manipulated_variables: We vary the preparation task that participants do before watching an instructional video. Participants either work through a solved problem (worked example) or try to find a solution on their own (inventing).
table.measured_variables:
We measure the following variables: 

learning outcome: We will measure the learning outcome after the instructional video with a post-test consisting of tasks on near transfer and far transfer of conceptual knowledge. 

Deep features: We will measure the processing of deep features with three measurements (think-aloud, recognition test and self-report). 
• Think-aloud: We will ask participants to speak-out their thoughts while working on the preparation task following the think-aloud procedure described by Ericsson & Simon, 1980. We will code the think-aloud protocols regarding the number of processed deep features as well as the level of processing of deep features. 
• Recognition test: We will measure the recognition of deep features with a recognition test after the preparation activity. The test consists of three items, each of which consists of three sets of images of diagrams. The sets are alienated variants of the original diagrams from the preparation activity. Each item contained only one set of diagrams that correctly represents a deep feature of the learning content (e.g., different number of data points). Participants are asked to decide which drawing most closely resembles the diagrams that were presented in the preparation phase. They are also asked to write a short explanation for their decision and to rate their certainty (on the scale very uncertain – uncertain – certain – very certain and the option “I guessed”).
• Self-report: We will measure the self-reported processing of deep features with a questionnaire at the end of the learning sequence. In this questionnaire, each deep feature is described, and participants are asked, if and when they first thought about that aspect. Therefore, they can choose one of the following options: “while working on the preparation task”, “during the questionnaire after the preparation activity”, “while working on the recognition task”, “while watching the instructional video”, “while working on the post-test”, “I never thought about this aspect”. 

We will also assess knowledge gap awareness, self-efficacy and epistemic curiosity using the questionnaires used in Glogger-Frey et al., 2015.
table.indices:
Learning outcome: We will sum up the achieved points in the post-test separately for near and for far transfer as measures for learning outcome. 

Deep Features – think-aloud: We will sum up the number of deep features that were elaborated. In addition, we will calculate the average level of processing for each participant. 

Deep Features – recognition test: We will count the number of correct recognitions. We will also count the number of correct reasoning of decisions. 

Deep Features – self-report: We will count the number of deep features that are self-reported as elaborated during the preparation activity.
table.statistical_tests:
Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity: 
We will calculate pearson correlation coefficients to analyse the convergent validity. We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of correctly recognized data sets in the recognition test and the number of correct reasoning in the recognition test (H1a). We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of self-reported elaborated deep features (H1b). 
In addition, we will check for differences of the correlation pattern between the inventing and the worked example subgroup and correct for them if necessary.

Difference Hypotheses 
We will use t-tests for two independent groups (Inventing vs. Worked Example) to analyse the differences in the number of elaborated deep features (H2a), recognition test score (H2b) and self-reported recognition of deep features (H2c)

Regression Hypotheses
We will run linear regression analyses with learning outcome (near transfer, far transfer) as dependent variables and deep features as independent variable. We will run separate regression analyses for each deep feature measurement (think-aloud, recognition test, self-report) as we expect a high correlation between them (multicollinearity). We expect similar result patterns for each deep feature measurement and will interpret this as an indicator of convergent validity.  
In addition, we will check for differences in the pattern of results between the inventing and worked example subgroups and correct for them if necessary.
table.transformations: We will code the think-aloud protocols as follows: In a first step, we will assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements. In a second step, we will determine the number of deep feature elements that were processed at a level of elaboration or higher.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p <.05 criteria for determining if the results significantly differ from those expected in the null hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants who report a lack of commitment will be excluded. Therefore, we have two control questions (one after the preparation activity and one after the post-test) in which participants are asked to rate their commitment. Participants who report less than 25% in one (or both) control questions will be excluded. 
We will also exclude participants who have problems with the think-aloud procedure (e.g. they seem very irritated/nervous about the procedure)
table.missing_data_handling: Only data from participants who completed the entire learning sequence will be included in the analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses: We plan to check for differences between the preparation activities regarding self-efficacy, epistemic curiosity and knowledge gap awareness for exploratory reasons.
table.additional_comments: We aim to use the data of this experiment to extend the sample size of another study where we could not reach the target sample size (see preregistration: https://osf.io/4tshq/?view_only=dfbdad9d7dca4e53940877d3daf9af21). Before merging the data, we will test whether the two subsamples differ systematically regarding age, gender and prior knowledge. We will only merge the data if there are no systematic differences between the subsamples.

2) Difference Hypotheses: Generally, we expect learners’ recognition of deep features to be higher in the worked example condition compared to learners in the inventing condition. More specifically:
2a) We expect that learners in the worked example condition elaborate more deep features (measured with think-aloud) compared to learners in the inventing condition.
2b) We expect that learners in the worked example condition reach a higher score in the developed recognition test compared to learners in the inventing condition.
2c) We expect that learners in the worked example condition self-report a higher recognition of deep features compared to learners in the inventing condition.

3) Regression Hypotheses: We expect that learners’ deep feature recognition (measured with think-aloud) predicts learning outcome (near transfer, H3a and far transfer, H3b).", "Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.", "For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.", "Between subjects design with 1 factor (preparation activity) and 2 levels (inventing task vs. self-explanation of worked example)", "Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two conditions.", "Registration prior to creation of data", "Participants will be recruited through advertisements in a first semester psychology lecture. Participants will receive a certificate of participation. Participants must be at least 18 years old and first year undergraduate students.", "Our target sample size is 100 participants.", "The target sample size ist based on power considerations as well as time and personnel factors: We expect to be able to assess approximately 100 participants within our time and personnel ressources. With this sample size we could achieve .97 power for the regression hypotheses (expecting a medium effect R^2 = .13, α = .05) and .99 power for the correlation hypotheses as well as .90 power for the difference hypotheses (α = .05, expected d = .60 based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022), which is acceptable to us.", "As we can only assess students at the beginning of their studies, the maximum possible sample size is determined by the number of first year psychology students willing to participate.", "We vary the preparation task that participants do before watching an instructional video. Participants either work through a solved problem (worked example) or try to find a solution on their own (inventing).", "We measure the following variables:

learning outcome: We will measure the learning outcome after the instructional video with a post-test consisting of tasks on near transfer and far transfer of conceptual knowledge.

Deep features: We will measure the processing of deep features with three measurements (think-aloud, recognition test and self-report).
• Think-aloud: We will ask participants to speak-out their thoughts while working on the preparation task following the think-aloud procedure described by Ericsson & Simon, 1980. We will code the think-aloud protocols regarding the number of processed deep features as well as the level of processing of deep features.
• Recognition test: We will measure the recognition of deep features with a recognition test after the preparation activity. The test consists of three items, each of which consists of three sets of images of diagrams. The sets are alienated variants of the original diagrams from the preparation activity. Each item contained only one set of diagrams that correctly represents a deep feature of the learning content (e.g., different number of data points). Participants are asked to decide which drawing most closely resembles the diagrams that were presented in the preparation phase. They are also asked to write a short explanation for their decision and to rate their certainty (on the scale very uncertain – uncertain – certain – very certain and the option “I guessed”).
• Self-report: We will measure the self-reported processing of deep features with a questionnaire at the end of the learning sequence. In this questionnaire, each deep feature is described, and participants are asked, if and when they first thought about that aspect. Therefore, they can choose one of the following options: “while working on the preparation task”, “during the questionnaire after the preparation activity”, “while working on the recognition task”, “while watching the instructional video”, “while working on the post-test”, “I never thought about this aspect”.

We will also assess knowledge gap awareness, self-efficacy and epistemic curiosity using the questionnaires used in Glogger-Frey et al., 2015.", "Learning outcome: We will sum up the achieved points in the post-test separately for near and for far transfer as measures for learning outcome.

Deep Features – think-aloud: We will sum up the number of deep features that were elaborated. In addition, we will calculate the average level of processing for each participant.

Deep Features – recognition test: We will count the number of correct recognitions. We will also count the number of correct reasoning of decisions.

Deep Features – self-report: We will count the number of deep features that are self-reported as elaborated during the preparation activity.", "Correlation Hypotheses – convergent validity:
We will calculate pearson correlation coefficients to analyse the convergent validity. We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of correctly recognized data sets in the recognition test and the number of correct reasoning in the recognition test (H1a). We will correlate the number of elaborated deep features (think-aloud) with the number of self-reported elaborated deep features (H1b).
In addition, we will check for differences of the correlation pattern between the inventing and the worked example subgroup and correct for them if necessary.

Difference Hypotheses
We will use t-tests for two independent groups (Inventing vs. Worked Example) to analyse the differences in the number of elaborated deep features (H2a), recognition test score (H2b) and self-reported recognition of deep features (H2c)

Regression Hypotheses
We will run linear regression analyses with learning outcome (near transfer, far transfer) as dependent variables and deep features as independent variable. We will run separate regression analyses for each deep feature measurement (think-aloud, recognition test, self-report) as we expect a high correlation between them (multicollinearity). We expect similar result patterns for each deep feature measurement and will interpret this as an indicator of convergent validity.
In addition, we will check for differences in the pattern of results between the inventing and worked example subgroups and correct for them if necessary.", "We will code the think-aloud protocols as follows: In a first step, we will assess the level of processing achieved for each of the four deep feature elements. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .809", "ps > .234", "ps > .444", 
"ps > .462"), Text = c("We found no significant differences in learners' self-rated prior knowledge regarding the variance formula or measures of dispersion, both Us < 595.00, both Zs < -0.24, both ps > .809 (two-tailed).", 
"Learners' self-reported commitment during preparation and while working on the posttest was high (see Table 3) and did not differ between conditions, both ts (67) < -1.21, both ps > .234 (two-tailed).", 
"We found no significant difference in learners' self-rated prior knowledge regarding the variance formula or measures of dispersion, both Us < 173.00, both Zs < -0.76, both ps > .444 (two-tailed).", 
"Learners' self-reported commitment while preparing and while working on the posttest did not differ between conditions, both ts (37) < -0.75, both ps > .462 (two-tailed)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 180 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("dataStudy1.sav", "dataStudy1.sav", "dataStudy1.sav", "dataStudy2.sav", "dataStudy2.sav", "dataStudy2.sav", "dataStudy2.sav" ), Column = c("RT1_reason", "RT2_reason", "RT3_reason", "PT05_answer", "PT07_answer", "PT08_answer", "commentsParticipant"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 247 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 168 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 167 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 134 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 184 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 193 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 194 characters, 100% distinct) may contain..." )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
-  3 installable dependencies detected.
- 682 statistics stored from the extracted output; 13 of 154 reported tests matched (8.4%).

ethics_statements: The experiment was approved by the university's ethics board and preregistered at OSF (https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba).
The experiment was approved by the university's ethics board and preregistered at OSF (https://osf.io/wajne/overview?view_only=9f4ae2374f204f69bb861d041db8a398).
live_data_statements: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions.
All participants were psychology students at a German university in their first semester of a Bachelor's degree program.
They received course credit for their participation and gave informed consent before taking part.

Participants were instructed to self-explain the presented solution and give the thoughts of a fictional classmate instead of producing a solution on their own (cf. Glogger-Frey et al., 2015; Glogger-Frey et al., 2017; Schalk et al., 2018).
Participants were asked to decide which set of diagrams most closely resembled the original diagrams from the preparation task and to briefly provide their reasoning for their decision.

In the questionnaire, each of the four deep features and its relevance were described in two or three sentences, and participants were asked if and when they had thought about this aspect for the first time, for example: 'When estimating the variance of a distribution, it is not sufficient to consider only the distribution's extreme points, as this will not produce accurate results.
Participants gave their answer by choosing one of these options.
Participants had 25 minutes to work on the tasks while speaking aloud all their thoughts.
Then participants had 20 minutes to complete the posttest with single-choice items presented on the computer screen and open items presented in a paper-pencil format.
Finally, participants completed the stimulated self-report.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions and either invented a solution (high-generative, n = 19) or self-explained a worked-out solution (low-generative, n = 20).
As in Study 1, all participants were psychology students at a German university in the first semester of a Bachelor's degree program and received course credit for their participation.
All participants gave informed consent before taking part.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `C:/xx/dataStudy2Imputation.sav` to `dataStudy2Imputation.sav` (in Study2Analyses_PTnear_imputated.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: MEASURING INTERMEDIATE DEEP FEATURE KNOWLEDGE IN PREPARATION-FOR-LEARNING

text.text: In preparation-for-learning, preparation activities can be designed differently and may foster different cognitive processes, resulting in different intermediate knowledge.

To understand how preparation-for-learning works and what makes it effective, different kinds of intermediate knowledge must be assessed, but it is challenging and time-consuming to measure intermediate deep-feature knowledge without influencing the learning process itself.
We tested two newly developed instruments for measuring intermediate deep-feature knowledge (recognition test, stimulated self-report) in two studies.
Correlations between the results from each instrument and a think-aloud measure were used as indicators of convergent validity.
Sensitivity was assessed by comparing two preparation activities (high-generative vs. lowgenerative).
In Study 1 (N = 69), neither the stimulated self-report nor the recognition test detected differences between the preparation activities in contrast to the think-aloud measure.
The stimulated self-report score was moderately correlated with the think-aloud measure.
The recognition test score was not correlated with the think-aloud measure.
On the basis of the Study 1 findings, adapted versions of the instruments were tested in Study 2 (N = 39).
In line with the results from the think-aloud measure, only the stimulated self-report was more sensitive at detecting better intermediate deep-feature knowledge in the low-generative condition.
The selfreport score was also significantly correlated with the think-aloud score, whereas the recognition test score was not.
Findings suggest that a stimulated self-report with well-designed response options can serve as a nonreactive, sensitive, and valid instrument for measuring intermediate deep-feature knowledge.
Preparation-for-learning is an instructional approach that combines a problem-solving task with subsequent expository instruction.
This sequence prepares learners to learn from this instruction by initiating learning-relevant cognitive processes such as the activation and generation of prior knowledge (Schwartz & Martin, 2004).
text.formatted: This sequence prepares learners to learn from this instruction by initiating learning-relevant cognitive processes such as the activation and generation of prior knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Schwartz & Martin, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The preparation material often contains contrasting cases that are designed to highlight distinctive deep features of the learning content (e.g., small data sets highlighting important features of dispersion) combined with an invention task (Schwartz & Bransford, 1998; Schwartz et al., 2011; Schwartz & Martin, 2004).
text.formatted: The preparation material often contains contrasting cases that are designed to highlight distinctive deep features of the learning content (e.g., small data sets highlighting important features of dispersion) combined with an invention task <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schwartz & Bransford, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schwartz et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schwartz & Martin, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This task requires learners to generate a method or formula (e.g., to describe the dispersion of given data points) by comparing the contrasting cases.

Such a problem-solving task initiates (meta-)cognitive processes such as prior-knowledge activation, knowledge-gap awareness, and recognition of deep features of the learning content (Loibl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Such a problem-solving task initiates (meta-)cognitive processes such as prior-knowledge activation, knowledge-gap awareness, and recognition of deep features of the learning content <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Loibl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These preparatory processes result in intermediate knowledge about the learning content, which forms the basis for learning from subsequent instruction and the acquisition of target knowledge (cf.
CID framework; Loibl et al., 2025).
text.formatted: CID framework; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Loibl et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Intermediate knowledge includes different kinds of cognitive and metacognitive knowledge related to the learning content, such as activated prior knowledge (cf. Brand et al., 2025), components of the target knowledge (deep features), erroneous knowledge, and knowledge about one's own knowledge gaps (Loibl et al., 2025)
text.formatted: Intermediate knowledge includes different kinds of cognitive and metacognitive knowledge related to the learning content, such as activated prior knowledge (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Brand et al., 2025)</ref>, components of the target knowledge (deep features), erroneous knowledge, and knowledge about one's own knowledge gaps <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Loibl et al., 2025)</ref>

text.text: It has been theorised that deep-feature recognition is an underlying mechanism of preparation-for-learning (Loibl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It has been theorised that deep-feature recognition is an underlying mechanism of preparation-for-learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Loibl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Deep features are crucial components of the target knowledge, and the term refers to the underlying, deeper structure of the learning content (e.g., an underlying physics law; Chi et al., 1981).
text.formatted: Deep features are crucial components of the target knowledge, and the term refers to the underlying, deeper structure of the learning content (e.g., an underlying physics law; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chi et al., 1981)</ref>.

text.text: For example, when the target knowledge is the standard deviation formula and an understanding of the underlying concept of variance, one deep feature is that the sample sizes of data sets need to be considered (by dividing by N) to enable comparisons between distributions with different sample sizes.

Processing this deep feature during preparation makes it more likely that learners' intermediate knowledge will include this component of the target knowledge, thereby building a basis for learning in the next instructional phase (Loibl et al., 2025; Schwartz & Martin, 2004).
text.formatted: Processing this deep feature during preparation makes it more likely that learners' intermediate knowledge will include this component of the target knowledge, thereby building a basis for learning in the next instructional phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Loibl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schwartz & Martin, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The acquired intermediate knowledge about deep features can help learners focus on relevant aspects and understand the target knowledge more deeply (Loibl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The acquired intermediate knowledge about deep features can help learners focus on relevant aspects and understand the target knowledge more deeply <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Loibl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In Glogger-Frey et al. (2022), student teachers invented quality criteria for evaluating a learning strategy via contrasting cases.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Glogger-Frey et al. (2022)</ref>, student teachers invented quality criteria for evaluating a learning strategy via contrasting cases.

text.text: Although intermediate knowledge was not measured directly, think-aloud data collected during the instructional phase revealed differences in the application of the canonical solution, indicating differences in the acquired intermediate deep-feature knowledge, which in turn mediated learning outcomes. Ockl and Glogger-Frey (2026) found that intermediate deep-feature knowledge, as measured via think-aloud during preparation, mediated the effect of preparation on near transfer.
text.formatted: Although intermediate knowledge was not measured directly, think-aloud data collected during the instructional phase revealed differences in the application of the canonical solution, indicating differences in the acquired intermediate deep-feature knowledge, which in turn mediated learning outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ockl and Glogger-Frey (2026)</ref> found that intermediate deep-feature knowledge, as measured via think-aloud during preparation, mediated the effect of preparation on near transfer.

text.text: Taken together, the mechanism of recognising deep features explains how working on a preparation task helps learners develop intermediate knowledge about key aspects of the learning content, which positively affects further learning processes and learning outcomes (Loibl et al., 2025; Loibl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Taken together, the mechanism of recognising deep features explains how working on a preparation task helps learners develop intermediate knowledge about key aspects of the learning content, which positively affects further learning processes and learning outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Loibl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Loibl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Intermediate deep-feature knowledge thus seems to be a mechanism of preparation-for-learning.
Investigating the underlying learning mechanisms of preparation-for-learning requires valid measures of intermediate knowledge.

A valid measure has good convergent validity, meaning that its scores correlate with scores from other instruments measuring the same or a related construct (Braun et al., 2012; Carlson & Herdman, 2012).
text.formatted: A valid measure has good convergent validity, meaning that its scores correlate with scores from other instruments measuring the same or a related construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Braun et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Carlson & Herdman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As substantial increases in divergent findings between different measures are associated with lower convergent validity, convergent validity less than r = .50 should be avoided (Carlson & Herdman, 2012).
text.formatted: As substantial increases in divergent findings between different measures are associated with lower convergent validity, convergent validity less than r = .50 should be avoided <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Carlson & Herdman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Besides convergent validity, the measure should also be sensitive to changes and differences due to treatments or interventions (Clark, 1988).
text.formatted: Besides convergent validity, the measure should also be sensitive to changes and differences due to treatments or interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Clark, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, the measure should be sensitive to differences that are usually found between high-generative preparation activities that require the generation of a solution and less generative activities that do not require a solution to be generated.

Less generative activities, such as observing a (failed) solution attempt (vicarious failure; Kapur, 2014) or working through a worked-out solution of the same problem (much like a 'woked example'; Glogger-Frey et al., 2015), can induce similar or higher levels of deep-feature processing than highly generative preparation activities.
text.formatted: Less generative activities, such as observing a (failed) solution attempt (vicarious failure; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kapur, 2014)</ref> or working through a worked-out solution of the same problem (much like a 'woked example'; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glogger-Frey et al., 2015)</ref>, can induce similar or higher levels of deep-feature processing than highly generative preparation activities.

text.text: In particular, preparation using worked examples has been shown to foster deeper processing of deep features compared with preparation using high-generative tasks (Glogger-Frey et al., 2022; Ockl & Glogger-Frey, 2026; Roelle & Berthold, 2015).
text.formatted: In particular, preparation using worked examples has been shown to foster deeper processing of deep features compared with preparation using high-generative tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Glogger-Frey et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ockl & Glogger-Frey, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Roelle & Berthold, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, a measure of intermediate deep-feature knowledge should be sensitive to detect differences between preparation tasks requiring high versus low levels of generation.
In addition, it is important to consider how to accurately measure intermediate deepfeature knowledge without influencing the learning process itself.
For instance, conducting a knowledge test after preparation to assess intermediate knowledge may influence the learning process through testing effects (Rowland, 2014).
text.formatted: For instance, conducting a knowledge test after preparation to assess intermediate knowledge may influence the learning process through testing effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Rowland, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In the case of deep features, directly asking for them would clearly enhance recognition of these features.
Therefore, a question that arises is: How can intermediate deep-feature knowledge be measured without influencing the actual learning process, but with good sensitivity and convergent validity?

Previous studies have usually looked at either the quality or quantity of solution attempts during the preparation phase as a proxy for measuring deep-feature processing and whether these aspects became part of intermediate knowledge (e.g., Brand et al., 2023; Hartmann et al., 2022; Loibl et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous studies have usually looked at either the quality or quantity of solution attempts during the preparation phase as a proxy for measuring deep-feature processing and whether these aspects became part of intermediate knowledge (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Brand et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hartmann et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Loibl et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The advantage of this approach is that it can easily be adapted to other tasks and materials, as long as they involve generating a solution that can be coded.
If they do not involve generating a solution (e.g., worked examples as preparation), it does not work.
And even for tasks that require solution attempts, coding them might be inaccurate, as coding only reflects processes that result in a written solution attempt.
For example, one might recognise a deep feature and elaborate on it but struggle to include it in a solution.
Nevertheless, the cognitive processes while elaborating should influence the intermediate deep-feature knowledge.

Another approach for measuring deep features is a recall drawing test in which students are asked to recall and draw the material from the preparation phase, that is, the contrasting cases (e.g., the clowns in buses as in Glogger-Frey et al., 2015; Glogger-Frey et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Another approach for measuring deep features is a recall drawing test in which students are asked to recall and draw the material from the preparation phase, that is, the contrasting cases (e.g., the clowns in buses as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glogger-Frey et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glogger-Frey et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schwartz et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The basic idea is that if the drawing correctly reflects a deep feature, then that feature must have been processed during preparation and has therefore become part of the participants' intermediate knowledge.
For example, if learners considered the ratio of clowns to bus compartments during preparation, their drawing should correctly depict this ratio.
The advantage of this approach is that it is suitable for a broader range of preparation tasks involving invention, productive failure, and worked examples or vicarious failure.

The recall test has been shown to be able to detect differences in deep-feature knowledge between preparation tasks (Glogger-Frey et al., 2017) or sequences (preparation first vs. instruction first; Schwartz et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The recall test has been shown to be able to detect differences in deep-feature knowledge between preparation tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Glogger-Frey et al., 2017)</ref> or sequences (preparation first vs. instruction first; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schwartz et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, the test also has limitations.
It cannot easily be transferred to materials without graphical or pictorial contrasting cases (but tables as in most productive failure studies, e.g., Kapur, 2014).
text.formatted: It cannot easily be transferred to materials without graphical or pictorial contrasting cases (but tables as in most productive failure studies, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kapur, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Even if the material allows for adaption, it remains difficult to distinguish between recall of deep features and recall of surface features.
For example, one might simply remember the correct position of the data points shown in a diagram without processing any deep features.
In this case, the drawing would accurately depict the deep feature, even though the participant did not elaborate on that aspect, meaning that it is not part of their intermediate knowledge.

In addition, as graphical representations are recalled relatively easily in immediate free recall tests (Bainbridge et al., 2019), this measurement approach requires a delay (as in Glogger-Frey et al., 2015; Glogger-Frey et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2011), which actually changes the instructional design and expected learning processes.
text.formatted: In addition, as graphical representations are recalled relatively easily in immediate free recall tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bainbridge et al., 2019)</ref>, this measurement approach requires a delay (as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glogger-Frey et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glogger-Frey et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schwartz et al., 2011)</ref>, which actually changes the instructional design and expected learning processes.

text.text: Therefore, we adapted the basic idea of the recall test using figures from the material, but instead of recalling them, the figures had to be recognised.
As we could hold the surface features constant within the figures used in the test, recognition based on these features was not possible and was thereby avoided.

Therefore, in this study, we designed a recognition test that presented defamiliarised figures that correctly depicted a deep feature from the preparation task alongside defamiliarised figures that did not depict the deep feature.
Learners were then asked to choose the figure that most closely resembled the original.

The basic idea is similar to that of a recall test: If learners have elaborated on a deep feature and it has become part of their intermediate knowledge, they should recognise the correct figure, even if it is defamiliarised.

We expected the recognition test to detect differences in the elaboration of deep features during different preparation tasks with at least the same sensitivity as a recall test but without the risk of interpreting surface recall as deep-feature recall.
A more direct way to investigate thoughts and cognitive processes is through verbal reports (Ericsson & Simon, 1980).
text.formatted: A more direct way to investigate thoughts and cognitive processes is through verbal reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ericsson & Simon, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the think-aloud method uses verbal protocols and asks learners to speak out all their thoughts while working on a task (van Someren et al., 1994).
text.formatted: For example, the think-aloud method uses verbal protocols and asks learners to speak out all their thoughts while working on a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(van Someren et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The transcribed protocols can be used to derive the construction of intermediate knowledge by coding the processing of deep features during preparation, which has demonstrated the sensitivity to detect differences between preparation tasks (cf. Ockl & Glogger-Frey, 2026).
text.formatted: The transcribed protocols can be used to derive the construction of intermediate knowledge by coding the processing of deep features during preparation, which has demonstrated the sensitivity to detect differences between preparation tasks (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ockl & Glogger-Frey, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: If implemented correctly, the think-aloud procedure is a valid measurement method that does not affect the cognitive processes themselves (Fox et al., 2011).
text.formatted: If implemented correctly, the think-aloud procedure is a valid measurement method that does not affect the cognitive processes themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fox et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Its validity can be enhanced and its reactivity minimised by providing proper instructions (e.g. speak out all thoughts continuously without planning or explaining, even if they are unrelated to the task; Ericsson & Simon, 1993) and training participants to think aloud (Hu & Gao, 2017).
text.formatted: Its validity can be enhanced and its reactivity minimised by providing proper instructions (e.g. speak out all thoughts continuously without planning or explaining, even if they are unrelated to the task; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ericsson & Simon, 1993)</ref> and training participants to think aloud <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hu & Gao, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, as the entire think-aloud process must be continuously monitored by an experimenter, and the recorded protocols must be transcribed prior to coding, implementing a think-aloud measure can be challenging and time-consuming.
Consequently, this method is resource-intensive, particularly with larger sample sizes or outside the laboratory.
Another method of assessing cognitive activities that uses verbal reports is called stimulated recall.
The basic idea is that a stimulus related to a particular situation will stimulate participants to recall their thoughts at that time (Gass & Mackey, 2013).
text.formatted: The basic idea is that a stimulus related to a particular situation will stimulate participants to recall their thoughts at that time <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gass & Mackey, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: To stimulate the recall, the situation or event of interest is typically recorded on video, and passages are replayed to the participant during an interview about their thoughts (Lyle, 2003).
text.formatted: To stimulate the recall, the situation or event of interest is typically recorded on video, and passages are replayed to the participant during an interview about their thoughts <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Lyle, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: However, because stimulated recall still involves an interview, as well as its transcription and coding, it remains timeconsuming and impractical for large sample sizes.

Thus, instead of combining stimulated recall with an interview, we borrowed the idea of stimulating the recall of a situation, namely, the phases of a study, and combined it with a self-report questionnaire asking learners to assess whether and when they had processed a deep feature throughout the learning sequence.
If implemented at the end of a learning sequence, it avoids the risk of influencing the learning process and producing a testing effect.

However, it is an open question whether learners can accurately estimate their intermediate deep-feature knowledge, given that self-assessed knowledge tends to correlate only modestly or even poorly with objective performance (Dunning et al., 2004).
text.formatted: However, it is an open question whether learners can accurately estimate their intermediate deep-feature knowledge, given that self-assessed knowledge tends to correlate only modestly or even poorly with objective performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dunning et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: But combining self-reports with stimulated recall should make it more accurate, thereby enhancing its correlation with a think-aloud measure and, consequently, its convergent validity.
In two studies, we tested and validated two instruments (recognition test and stimulated self-report) for measuring intermediate deep-feature knowledge.

In order to assess the sensitivity of these instruments, we also compared intermediate deep-feature knowledge after preparation with a high-generative activity (invention) versus a low-generative activity (worked example).
In addition, we also investigated the relationship between intermediate deep-feature knowledge and learning outcomes, that is, the predictive validity of the instrument.

We tested the following preregistered hypotheses (https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba): (1) Correlational hypotheses -convergent validity: Intermediate deep-feature knowledge measured with the think-aloud procedure will be strongly positively correlated with the recognition test score (1a) and the stimulated self-report score (1b).
text.formatted: We tested the following preregistered hypotheses (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba">https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba</ref>): (1) Correlational hypotheses -convergent validity: Intermediate deep-feature knowledge measured with the think-aloud procedure will be strongly positively correlated with the recognition test score (1a) and the stimulated self-report score (1b).

text.text: (2) Difference hypotheses -sensitivity: Learners in the low-generative worked example condition will show more elaborated deep-feature knowledge in the think-aloud measure (2a), the recognition test (2b), and the stimulated self-report (2c) than learners in the high-generative invention condition.

(3) Regression hypotheses -predictive validity: Learners' intermediate deep-feature knowledge measured with the think-aloud procedure (3a), the recognition test (3b), and stimulated self-report (3c) predicts learning outcomes (near and far transfer).foot_0
text.formatted: (3) Regression hypotheses -predictive validity: Learners' intermediate deep-feature knowledge measured with the think-aloud procedure (3a), the recognition test (3b), and stimulated self-report (3c) predicts learning outcomes (near and far transfer).<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref>

text.text: The study followed a one-factorial design, with the generativity of the preparation activity as the between-subjects factor.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions.
They either invented a solution (high-generative, n = 35) or selfexplained a worked-out solution (low-generative, n = 34).
All participants were psychology students at a German university in their first semester of a Bachelor's degree program.
They received course credit for their participation and gave informed consent before taking part.
We measured intermediate deep-feature knowledge in three ways (think-aloud, recognition test, and stimulated self-report).
The experiment was approved by the university's ethics board and preregistered at OSF (https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba).
text.formatted: The experiment was approved by the university's ethics board and preregistered at OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba">https://osf.io/2j6t8/overview?view_only=81b5529f0e074d2cb437a8c354f2ecba</ref>).

text.text: We expected a large effect size for the correlational hypotheses (r = .50), a medium effect size for the regression hypotheses (R² = .12), and d = 0.60 (based on Glogger-Frey et al., 2022) for the difference hypotheses.
Based on these a priori power considerations, the target sample size was N = 100 in order to achieve at least .90 power.
Initially, 77 first-year students participated in the experiment.

We excluded eight participants due to technical issues or problems with the think-aloud procedure or preregistered criteria, namely, a reported lack of commitment, resulting in 69 valid cases (83% female; 16% male, 1% nonbinary; age: M = 20.2, SD = 2.4).
With N = 69, we could still achieve an acceptable power of ≥ .80 for all analyses.
Preparation Task.
The learning material for the preparation phase was experimentally varied.

In both experimental groups, the material consisted of three contrasting cases in the expect similar result patterns for each deep-feature measure and will interpret this similarity as an indicator of convergent validity.

However, we failed to preregister separate hypotheses for the stimulated self-report and the recognition test and originally preregistered only the following regression hypotheses: We expect that learners' deep-feature recognition (measured with the think-aloud procedure) will predict the learning outcomes (near transfer, H3a; far transfer, H3b).

text.text: Before coding, all expressed thoughts were recorded and transcribed using the AI-based transcription software noScribe (Dröge, 2023).
text.formatted: Before coding, all expressed thoughts were recorded and transcribed using the AI-based transcription software noScribe <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dröge, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Student assistants carefully checked and corrected the raw transcripts generated by the software.

They then coded the following deep features: (a) inclusion of all data points, (b) deviations from the mean (fixed reference point), (c) squared or absolute deviations, and (d) dividing by the number of data points.
The deep features were derived from the four functional components of the standard deviation formula described by Loibl et al. (2020).

text.text: The level of processing of each deep feature was coded on a scale ranging from 0 (not mentioned) to 4 (elaboration + correct mathematical solution) within the protocols as specified by the rating scheme described in Table 1.
text.formatted: The level of processing of each deep feature was coded on a scale ranging from 0 (not mentioned) to 4 (elaboration + correct mathematical solution) within the protocols as specified by the rating scheme described in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The final think-aloud score for intermediate deep-feature knowledge was the number of deep features that were processed at a level of elaboration (Level 3) or higher.
About 25% of the think-aloud protocol were doublecoded by three trained student assistants (ICC = .72).
The recognition test presented defamiliarised variants of the original diagrams from the preparation activity.

Each recognition test item targeted one deep feature derived from the functional components of the standard deviation formula described in Loibl et al. (2020)foot_1 and was based on the same principle: Each item consisted of three defamiliarised sets of diagrams and only one of them correctly represented the targeted deep feature (e.g., different number of data points as an approximation of the deep feature 'divide by N'), besides the other deep features.

text.text: Participants were asked to decide which set of diagrams most closely resembled the original diagrams from the preparation task and to briefly provide their reasoning for their decision.
Each deep feature was tested by one item, and participants could receive up to 2 points per deep feature (1 for a correct decision and 1 for the correct reasoning).
The coding of the reasoning followed a rating scheme (see Table 2).
